articleTitle: Editing in RDAT
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: RDAT is a high density digital audio recorder which uses a combination of high coercivity metal powder tape, azimuth recording and rotary heads to allow two channels of 16-bit digital audio to be recorded at a linear tape speed of only 8.15 mm/sec. The tape tracks produced by this helical scan format are only 13 micrometres wide, and an active track following system is necessary for replay. The details of the RDAT format have been documented elsewhere, and this paper confines itself to those aspects of RDAT which affect its use as an editing system for audio post production and Compact Disc mastering.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Error detecting runlength-limited sequences
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: Codes based on runlength-limited sequences are the state of the art corner stone of current disk recorders, whether their nature is magnetic or optical. The error detecting or correcting capabilities of runlength limited sequences are quite poor. In this paper, the author presents an algebraic approach for constructing runlength-limited block codes of fixed codeword length that impart some error detecting capabilities.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On the performance of symbol- and fractionally-spaced equalization in digital magnetic recording
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: Equalization is a mature technology in digital communications and is used in many applications to improve the spectral efficiency (bits/sec/Hz) of the channel and reduce sensitivity to channel variations. It has the same potential for digital magnetic recording systems and may be used to achieve similar benefits, namely, (1) higher storage density on available head/medium combinations, and (2) reduced performance sensitivity to variation in the readback signal resulting from manufacturing tolerances, etc. The purpose of this paper is to describe analytic and simulated results on the performance of digital equalization with partial response methods. Two partial response signals, namely, Class 4 (PR4) and extended-Class 4 (EPR4), are considered. The digital equalizer is configured as a transversal filter (also called finite impulse response, FIR, filter) that linearly combines a finite sequence of samples of the readback signal to form a desired output. The sampling interval equals either the symbol period or a fraction thereof, but the output is computed at the symbol rate, 1/T. The resulting approaches are referred to as synchronous and fractionally-spaced equalization (FSE) respectively.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Record and playback systems for 1.2 Gb/s HDTV digital VTR
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: Some of the essential technology of the record/playback system of a 1.2 Gb/s digital VTR are described. The VTR can record the full bandwidth of 1125/60 HDTV signals, namely, 30 MHz for luminance, and 15 MHz for each of the two color difference signals. Integrated detection and a 5-tap transversal filter appropriate to the developed head-tape systems with a cross-shaped multilayered amorphous head and metal particle tape, and a special PLL to cope with stunt motion are studied. At a high data rate of 148.5 Mb/s and a high linear density of 0.345 mu m per bit, the recorder confirms reliable operation with a word error rate of less than 10/sup -4/.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: New ADRC for consumer digital VCR
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: A bit rate reduction method for consumer digital VCR must meet special requirements such as fast motion playback, slow motion playback, and electronic editing, while keeping robustness for consumer use. Adaptive quantizing is the suitable method to remove redundancies in data within each pixel level while keeping robustness for error propagation, which is essential to the capability of error concealment and multiple-dubbing. Considering these requirements, the authors developed the ADRC (adaptive dynamic range coding) method which can remove level redundancy according to the dynamic range of the block. They have improved the quantizing ability of ADRC and the efficiency of 3-dimensional processing. For a further improvement of compression efficiency, the spatio-temporal subsampling method is introduced to combine with the ADRC method. Using this new coding method, one can compress the Y, R-Y, B-Y component signal to 12.5 Mbps while maintaining picture quality. They have confirmed the efficiency of the new ADRC method by computer simulation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A way to assess the performance of heads and tapes for digital video recording
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: The authors describe a method to express the magnetic recording channel performance with a single number: the performance indicator (PI). PI is derived from the signal-to-noise ratio at the detector of a digital system for partial response class IV detection using a simple analytical expression. PI can be used as a figure of merit for a head-tape combination. The relative performance of heads can now be assessed by using the same tape and comparing the PI values. Also the relative performance of different kinds of tapes using the same head can be evaluated. Date from MIG and Sandwich heads obtained at a head-to-tape velocity of a 5 m/s and using various tapes (VHS, SVHS, MP, ME) are shown.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Quadrature amplitude modulation recording for digital VCRs
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: To improve recording efficiency and increase the channel bit rate of VCRs, the authors studied the application of quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) to magnetic recording channels. Since QAM requires the channel to have a linear characteristic, bias recording was used to record the QAM signal. It was found with simulations that the QAM number '16' (16QAM) was suitable for VCRs. To increase channel bit rate or decrease required SNR, the 16QAM was modified to 32QAM with coded modulation technique (Trellis coding). Coded 32QAM signals of 30 Mbps data rate were recorded and reproduced with a word error rate less than 10E-4 using an experimental VCR having head scanning speed of 5.8 m/s, and track width of 20 mu m.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Sawtooth magnetisation transitions and the digital recording properties of thin film recording media
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: The authors discuss the nature of sawtooth magnetisation transitions, the process of recording which produces them, and their relationship to the magnetic hysteresis properties of the thin films in which they exist. They also consider the distributions of transition widths and these properties are related to the magnetic hysteresis properties of the media, and the origin of these hysteresis properties. It is shown that the recording properties of thin film media are substantially determined by the ratio M/sub r/D/H/sub c/ (remanent magnetisation*thickness/coercivity) in a way which is largely consistent with current understanding built upon considerations which ignore the superstructure within the transitions. A discussion is given of the theoretical predictions in the light of published experimental observations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Characterization and measurement of nonlinear bit shifts in digital magnetic tape recording
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: Nonlinearities (such as nonlinear bit shifts) are characterized in the form of nonlinear responses by Volterra series expansion. A least-squares procedure is developed to identify the linear and nonlinear responses simultaneously from measurements of the read-head response to some pseudo-random sequences written on tape. A number of experiments have been performed using a helical scan system at different drum speeds. Different MIG heads and metal evaporated (ME) and metal particle (MP) tapes have been used and different write-current levels have been tried out. The authors identifies nonlinear bit shifts quantitatively and shows that the most significant part of nonlinearities can be modelled by just a few parameters. From his measurements, he concludes that nonlinear bit shifts increase with increasing bit density, data rate and write current rise-time.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Channel capacity of DC-free ternary recording codes
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: High demand for an increase of packing density still lends motivation to the development of new robust recording codes. The study of ternary codes with charge-constraint is one of the interesting practical approaches for this purpose. Given bounds on the run-length and the accumulated charge under NRZL rule, the authors investigate the channel capacity of ordinary ternary recording codes. The results are tabulated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Broadcasters' use of optical discs for audio recording
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: Disc-based removeable recording media are well suited to audio recording, especially where the recordings might need minimal editing prior to their broadcasting. Optical technologies are well suited to archival applications since the recording is buried below the surface. In many other ways, the optical disc recording systems that are being developed for computer applications appear well suited to audio recording applications. It is not considered that the broadcaster's requirements are so much different from domestic or other industrial applications of the technology. Therefore, the potential of optical discs has been examined and some methods devised which might allow the broadcaster to capitalise on the development of this technology which is at present targeted to domestic and computer industry applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: SVHS-the development of an improved format
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: The author looks briefly at the developments applied to VHS leading up to the announcement of SVHS in 1987, before turning to the problems posed to the development team, given the brief to develop vastly superior performance whilst maintaining compatibility with the original system. He also looks at the solutions to these problems, covering various areas of technology in the video recorder and concentrating specifically on the tape formulation and on some new techniques applied to enhance the chrominance performance of the system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: 1/2-inch video cassette recorder for baseband HDTV
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: This paper reports on the details of the video and audio signal processing methods and system constitution of 1/2 inch cassette HDVTR, which has been developed satisfying the required specifications. The developed HDVTR employs a 20 MHz luminance signal and 7 MHz chrominance signal (line sequential), and four-channel digital audio recording system with a sampling frequency of 48 kHz and 16-bit linear quantization. The digital audio signals are recorded on the overlapped tape area to the video track by using the same heads employed for video recording. A laminated amorphous alloy head and metal particle tape are employed. The attained recording time is 63 minutes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Low complexity decoding for intersymbol interference channels
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: The author first discusses the performance of the M-algorithm for intersymbol interference (ISI) channels. As a specific example, he considers the magnetic recording channel for four different densities. If decoding error probability is the performance criterium, then he concludes that for this type of channel only a few estimates need to be considered by the decoder. He gives simulation results for a modified maximum likelihood sequence estimation (MLSE) decoding algorithm that uses a subset of the states as defined by the channel impulse response. Simulations results indicate that this type of decoding can be very efficient. He also shows that interleaving, combined with a minimum amount of redundancy, gives rise to surprisingly good decoding performance for a direct detection with soft decisions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Characterisation of a magneto-optic recording channel using a scanning laser microscope
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: The characterisation of a magneto-optic recording channel consisting of a scanning laser microscope and rare-earth/transition metal recording layers is described. The channel is treated in a linear manner and its step response determined both experimentally and theoretically. Agreement between the two is good.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Thin film M-R read/write devices
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: The author presents a feasibility study of a thin film read/write head with a magneto-resistive (M-R) film. A computer model of such a read/write head has been devised. Calculations of the recording and bias fields in the pole-to-recording medium space have been carried out; a mathematical model of a ring type head based on Karlqvist's x-component was used as the perpendicular field distribution function for the single pole head. An improved mathematical analysis of the single pole head is presented by dividing the potential distribution into two regions, one underneath and one around the pole. Computer software, written in Fortran, produces the relevant response curves and magnetic field plots for direct comparison with the results obtained on a large scale experimental model. The agreement is not perfect but it shows that the approximations made in the theory are entirely justified for most practical purposes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The measurement and classification of impairment for DVTR transports
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: The author discusses which of the many sources of impairment in the transports of digital video tape recorders (DVTR) are particularly important, and describes a method for resolving the overall impairment into these constituents. This method includes one stage of nonlinear analysis (of a potential family of nonlinear distortion mechanisms), and is implemented on a computer simulation system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High capacity, high reliability data storage
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: As the capacity of Winchester disks in computers continues to increase, so the capacity of tape backup is forced to keep step. Media based on iron oxide has been the mainstay of the secondary storage industry for several decades, but this form of media is now reaching the limit of its development. A new technology has been developed which will meet the needs of industry for many years to come. Building on the emerging digital audio tape (DAT) technology, the computer tape industry has made a leap in both capacity and data reliability to produce a product with great scope for improvement in the future. This paper describes the principle of rotating head technology, as it is applied to DAT. This is followed by a description of improvements made to bring the technology up to the high standard of operation required by the computer industry.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A run-length limited coding algorithm with DC control
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: Describes a simple coding algorithm suitable for rotary-head digital magnetic recording channels. Under this method, a family of run-length limited (RLL) modulation codes for (1-D) channels (i.e. precoded by NRZ-I rules) and (1-D/sup 2/) channels (i.e. precoded by interleaved NRZ-I rules) can be generated. For high-density recording, signal-to-noise ratio is low, jitter and phase shift are large, therefore, a modulation code with large window margin, is important. In the case of guardbandless recording, crosstalk noise from adjacent tracks is relatively high, hence, a small pulse width ratio, is favorable. The authors discuss a few examples of modulation codes constructed using the simple algorithm and show that code rate, pulse width ratio, and low-frequency suppression power can be compromised within the design rules.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Bitshift errors due to wideband noise in digital magnetic recording
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: An expression is derived for the PDF (probability density function) of the bitshift due to additive noise which assumes that the replay signal and the noise have comparable bandwidths. The error rate against signal-to-noise ratio characteristic is computed and it is shown that the effect of noise bitshift is more severe than is suggested by the usual error function expression for the error rate. Characteristics are compared for white and coloured noise at the differentiator input, and it is shown that at low packing densities the modified PDF for noise induced bitshift give error rates which more closely follow experimental results.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A review of noise in magneto-optic recording
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: The various sources of noise identified are discussed followed by a comparison of carrier-to-noise ratio (CNR) and SNR methods of characterising optical data channels. The various detection schemes and their relative merits are also discussed. Three main types of noise discussed are electronic noise, laser noise and media noise.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Non-destructive procedure for viewing formats on tape
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: Tape inspection would be simplified considerably by the use of a nondestructive process. In that way magneto-optical garnets must be considered as a significant improvement for reading the recorded tracks and checking compliance with the format. Magneto-optical readout heads allow both high data rate transfer and static imaging and are developed to play video and audio tapes and magnetic discs. Magnetic domains are energized by the leakage flux from the bit transition record on the medium. Vertical domains are optically detected using the Faraday rotation on the magnetic garnets. Growth processes by liquid phase epitaxy, and magnetic properties of thin film garnets are discussed. Some experimental results are commented on.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Spectral analysis of the read process (magnetic recording)
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: The transmission behavior of a head core is investigated experimentally. The frequency dependent complex efficiency has been measured via the impedance of the head. This method employs the assumption of approximative linearity of the head core magnetization under read process conditions. The determined contribution of the head core to the magnitude spectrum is negligible. The phase contribution adds asymmetry to the read pulse. A model is used for the analysis of the recording system with ring type head. Its application to finite pole length head type systems suggests itself. In addition it is conceivable to use the approach for the design of optimum magnetization distributions in multilayer media.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High-density magnetic recording: a driving force for HDTV?
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: Rotary digital magnetic tape recorders are being used for both audio (DAT), and for data (Exabyte 8 mm drive). In both of these commercially available products, the areal storage density approaches 100,000,000 bits/square inch at acceptable error rates. The characteristics of a helical-scan recorder with even higher areal densities designed for HDTV use is described. A complete digital HDTV system is described along with the constraints and requirements of the various functional components. In addition, the current state of HDTV being proposed in America is also described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Development of removable mass information storage through Bernoulli principle
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: Norton and Wright of IBM showed that the disc flutter problem could be solved by using the Bernoulli effect. In their proposed design the disc is rotated at a higher speed in close proximity to a fixed flat plate called the Bernoulli plate. This tends to create an air bearing between the disc and the plate and the floppy disc acts like a rigid plate. A slot in the Bernoulli plate allows magnetic head to access the disc. As the disc passes over the slot a pull-down force is exerted, also known as dimpling. This stabilizes the disc and keeps a constant spacing with the magnetic head. By radially extending the slot to the extremities of the floppy disc the entire area of the disc can be employed for recording. Utilizing the Bernoulli plate and introducing the head through a slot allows the opportunity to adjust the head-disc spacing for optimal signal amplitude.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Low-frequency suppression in RLL codes for optical recording
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: New demanding applications of write-once and erasable optical media for video and data storage, put high constraints on the signal-to-noise ratio in the servo loops and require channel codes with improved low-frequency characteristics. New run length limited (RLL) block codes for optical recording with higher suppression of the low-frequency components are presented. These result from new criteria and design features in the choice of the alphabet of the codewords, in the algorithms for the minimization of the low-frequency contents and in the merging procedure. Results of the spectra calculation according to the described design have shown very good improvements in the low-frequency contents of the EFM code. Other results of optimized d=2 codes, suitable for optical recording applications are reported.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Contour biasing and AC biasing-a comparison
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: In direct magnetic recording, the distortion mechanism has been measured and found to be essentially cubic in structure. Using the dual input describing function approach, a mathematical model describes the linearising effect of AC biasing which agrees very well with practice especially at long wavelengths. A new method of making distortion-free recording is proposed, called Contour Biasing. With the removal of AC bias, the majority of the high frequency losses disappear giving substantially improved performance at short wavelength. A new model of the recording process is proposed and three more distortion mechanisms are defined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A new single-table bit assignment technique for transform coded images
publicationTitle: 1990 Eighth International Conference on Video, Audio and Data Recording
abstract: Spatial transform coding with variable-length coding has been widely applied for image compression because of its high coding efficiency. The proposed bit-assignment techniques for such systems are mostly based on applying a plurality of encoding tables, as statistically different types of data have to be encoded. However, the multiplexing of codewords originated from various encoding tables considerably complicates the design of a self-synchronizing code. This paper describes a bit-assignment technique which makes use of a single encoding table while maintaining the coding efficiency. A self-synchronizing code suited for this algorithm will be presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
